lesson.title: OrderedDict: Order-Sensitive Equality and Moving Keys Around
lesson.summary: collections.OrderedDict is a dict subclass built specifically around ordering, offering methods like move_to_end and order-sensitive equality that a plain dict does not provide even though plain dicts have preserved insertion order since Python 3.7.
lesson.body:
OrderedDict lives in the same collections module you have already met, the standard library's home for specialized container types that extend or refine the built-in list, dict, and tuple. It raises an obvious question, though: since Python 3.7, regular dictionaries guarantee they preserve insertion order as an official language feature, the order you added keys is the order you get back when you iterate. So why does OrderedDict still exist, and why would you ever choose it over a plain dict?

The answer is that OrderedDict does more than simply preserve order, it treats order as data that you can actively manipulate and that participates in comparisons. It has a move_to_end method that lets you take an existing key and slide it to the front or back of the ordering without removing and re-adding it, useful for building things like a least-recently-used cache, where the most recently touched item needs to move to one end every time it is accessed. A plain dict has no equivalent method for reordering an existing key in place.

OrderedDict also changes what equality means. Two plain dicts are considered equal if they hold the same keys mapped to the same values, regardless of what order those keys were inserted in. Two OrderedDict instances, by contrast, are only equal to each other if both their contents and their order match. Comparing an OrderedDict to a plain dict, however, falls back to order-insensitive comparison, the same as two plain dicts. This distinction matters anywhere the sequence of items genuinely carries meaning, like a configuration file where operations must apply in the order they were written.

```python
from collections import OrderedDict

od = OrderedDict()
od["first"] = 1
od["second"] = 2
od["third"] = 3

od.move_to_end("first")
print(list(od.items()))

od2 = OrderedDict([("second", 2), ("third", 3), ("first", 1)])
print(od == od2)
```

od starts in the order first, second, third. Calling od.move_to_end("first") slides "first" to the back without touching second or third, leaving the order second, third, first. That is exactly the order od2 was built in, so the order-sensitive equality check passes. The output is:

```
[('second', 2), ('third', 3), ('first', 1)]
True
```

If you swapped od2 back to first, second, third order, the items would be identical but the equality check would return False, something a plain dict comparison could never do. Reach for OrderedDict specifically when your code needs to reorder existing keys or when the order of items is itself something you need to test for, otherwise a plain dict already gives you insertion order for free.
